chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from al-Sayyari, and al-Fadl ibn Abi Qurra, raising it, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

He was asked about the fifty-one rak'at, so he said: 'The hours of the day are twelve hours, and the hours of the night are twelve hours; and from the emergence of dawn to the emergence of the sun is one hour, and from the setting of the sun to the setting of the twilight is darkness (ghasaq), and for every hour two rak'at, and for the darkness one rak'at.'
ai.seo_question: How are the 51 daily prayers calculated based on hours of the day and night?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidates the structure of the fifty-one daily rak'at by mapping them to the twelve hours of day and night, assigning two rak'at per hour. This calculation accounts for specific transitional periods, such as the hour between dawn and sunrise and the twilight period (ghasaq) after sunset, providing a temporal framework for the obligatory and supererogatory prayers. This method reflects the Shia scholarly tradition of linking ritual acts to natural cosmic cycles, emphasizing the spiritual significance of time in worship.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Muhammad Bin Ahmad, from Al-Sayyari, from Al-Fazl Bin Abu Qurra, raising it, (It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullahasws, said, ‘Heasws was asked about the fifty one Rak’at (of daily Salāt).

So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘The hours of the day are twelve hours, and the hours of the night are twelve hours; and from the emergence of the dawn to the emergence of the sun is an hour, and from the setting of the sun to the setting of the twilight is darkness, and for every two hours are two Rak’at, and for the darkness, one Rak’at’.
en.sarwar: 5. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad from af-Sayyariy from af-Fadf ibn abu Qurrah in a in a marfu‘ manner who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, was asked about fifty-one Rak‘at Salah (prayer) daily.

He replied, ‘There are twelve hours in the day and twelve in the night. There is one hour between dawn and sunrise. From sunset to disappearing of western brightness is darkness. For every hour there are two Rak‘at and one Rak‘at for darkness.’”
